passage:
My roommate Nilesh spent two months planning his first home-bakery stall at the Sunday flea market in Pune. On the day, it drizzled, half the crowd never came, and he carried three boxes of unsold brownies back up our stairs.

"Total disaster," he said, dropping onto the sofa. "I'm not a baker. I'm a guy who wasted two months."

Then he went quiet and frowned at the ceiling. "No. Disaster is too big a word." He took a flattened pizza box and drew a line from one to ten. Sales: four. The lemon cake sold out in an hour, so that was a nine. Stall set-up: two, because the banner kept blowing into people's faces. Price cards: seven.

I didn't say much. I just watched him make two lists, "Keep" and "Change", in black marker. The "Keep" list was longer.

"So maybe a five," he said. "And next time, a heavier banner and more lemon cake."

— Tarun

qa.q: What sold out in an hour at Nilesh's stall?
qa.a: The lemon cake sold out in an hour.

qa.q: Why did "total disaster" feel accurate to Nilesh as he dropped onto the sofa?
qa.a: He was tired, wet and carrying three boxes of unsold brownies, so the losses were all he could see. After two months of planning, anything less than success felt like wasted time.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and why did the scale help?
qa.a: The turning point was when Nilesh caught himself and said disaster was too big a word. Rating each part from one to ten showed what worked, like the lemon cake, and gave clear fixes for next time.

qa.q: How might Tarun have felt watching Nilesh go from "disaster" to "maybe a five"?
qa.a: Tarun was probably relieved to see a friend stop beating himself up without needing to be argued out of it. Staying quiet and just watching let Nilesh do the rethinking himself.

grounding: A roommate watches a young man catch himself calling his market stall a disaster, then rate each part on a scale and list what worked and what to change.

passage:
Friday: Charu pressed "submit" at 11:52 p.m. Her bus-shelter design for the city competition had taken four months of evenings. She lay awake picturing her name on the winners' board.

Monday, 10 a.m.: The list came out. Not even shortlisted. Charu closed her laptop. "It was all rubbish. Four months of rubbish," she told Lavanya at the next desk, and went to stand at the office window for a long time.

Wednesday evening: At home, Charu opened the file again, mostly to delete it. Instead she caught her own words: all rubbish. Was it? She made a grid. Idea: eight out of ten; the rainwater roof was good. Drawings: six. Cost estimate: three, rushed at the end. Written statement: four, too long.

She wrote at the bottom: "Next time, start the costing in month two." Then she saved the file under a new name: "Round 2".

qa.q: What did Charu give the rainwater roof idea?
qa.a: Charu gave the idea eight out of ten.

qa.q: What might Charu have been feeling as she stood at the office window for a long time?
qa.a: She was probably crushed and embarrassed after four months of evenings, and her words suggest she felt the whole effort was worthless. Standing alone gave her space to hide it.

qa.q: Which choice on Wednesday changed what Charu took from the competition?
qa.a: Instead of deleting the file, she questioned her own phrase "all rubbish" and graded each part. That showed a strong idea and a weak cost estimate, which she can fix next time.

qa.q: What would change if Lavanya had agreed on Monday that it was all rubbish?
qa.a: Charu might have deleted the file on Wednesday and never seen what was good about it. Lavanya's silence, at least, didn't lock in the harsh verdict.

grounding: Over three days a young woman goes from calling her competition entry all rubbish to grading its parts and noting what to change next time.

On the school bus in Delhi, Lokesh unzipped his bag and saw it: no EVS project file. It was still on the dining table, next to the fruit bowl.

His fingers went cold. Ma'am will be so angry. She'll send me to the principal. The principal will cane me, like in Dadaji's old stories. Then they'll throw me out. Everyone will know, forever.

Baljeet, beside him, looked up. "What happened?"

"I forgot my project file," Lokesh whispered. "I'm finished."

In class, he went to Ma'am's desk first, voice shaking. Ma'am looked up from the register. "Bring it tomorrow, Lokesh. Write it in your diary."

That was all. He walked back feeling light and a bit silly.

qa.q: Where had Lokesh left his EVS project file?
qa.a: It was still on the dining table, next to the fruit bowl.

qa.q: Why did "I'm finished" feel true to Lokesh on the bus?
qa.a: In his head, each step followed the last so quickly, from Ma'am's anger to the principal to a new school, that the worst ending felt certain. The cold fingers show how real the fear was.

qa.q: What small step helped Lokesh, and what could he try the next time his mind races?
qa.a: Going to Ma'am's desk first and telling her let him find out what really happens. Next time he could ask himself, "What usually happens when someone forgets?" before believing the worst.

qa.a: Baljeet might find it strange or even a bit funny that a forgotten file means being "finished". Baljeet could help by reminding Lokesh what happened last time someone forgot.

Bhaiya, you asked why I was so weird on Saturday. Okay. I'm Nilesh, I'm fifteen, and I'm a bit dramatic. Here's what happened.

I sent Tarun a message at four: "coming for cricket?" Blue ticks. No reply. Five o'clock, nothing. By six I'd worked it out. He's angry because I dropped his catch on Thursday. He's told Imran. Imran's told the whole group. They've made a new chat without me. On Monday nobody will sit with me at lunch.

Each step felt like a fact. I even started deciding where I'd sit alone.

At nine, Tarun called. "Sorry yaar, I read it on the bus and then we went to my nani's village, zero network." That's it. He hadn't even remembered the catch.

What gets me is how sure I was. I didn't know anything. I just had one blue tick and a lot of fear.

qa.q: When did Tarun call Nilesh?
qa.a: At nine, Tarun called.

qa.q: Why did each step feel like a fact to Nilesh, even though it wasn't?
qa.a: Nilesh was scared, and fear filled the silence with the worst explanations, linking them into a chain that seemed logical. The dropped catch gave the story something real to hang on.

qa.q: What could Nilesh try next time a friend goes quiet?
qa.a: Notice the chain as it starts and list other simple reasons for no reply, like travel or no network. Waiting a bit, or sending one light message, is better than planning where to sit alone.

qa.q: How might Tarun have felt if Nilesh had skipped cricket and ignored him on Monday?
qa.a: Tarun would probably have been confused and hurt, since he hadn't even remembered the catch. Nilesh's fear could have created the very distance Nilesh was afraid of.

grounding: A fifteen-year-old tells Bhaiya how one unanswered message led to certainty that a friend was angry and the whole group hated Nilesh, until the friend called.

I'm Lavanya, Charu's older sister. I'm writing this down because I don't want to forget how fast it happened.

Tuesday after school, Charu, fourteen, sent her best friend Mitali a long voice note about a new song. By dinner there was no reply. Charu kept checking the phone under the table. Amma asked her twice to pass the rasam and she didn't hear.

At nine she came to my room and sat on the floor. "Mitali's ignoring me. She's bored of me. She probably laughed with Keerthi about my voice note. They'll sit together tomorrow and I'll be on my own." She said it like reading the news.

I don't know exactly what was in her head. But her knees were pulled up tight, and she didn't cry, which is worse with Charu.

At 9:40 her phone buzzed. Mitali: "sorry!! tuition ran late, listening now 🎧" Charu laughed, and then looked embarrassed for laughing.

qa.q: What did Amma ask Charu to pass at dinner?
qa.a: Amma asked her twice to pass the rasam.

qa.q: What does Charu saying it "like reading the news" suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: She seemed completely sure that Mitali was bored of her and that she'd be alone, even though nothing had happened yet. The fear felt like fact, not a guess.

qa.q: How could Lavanya help Charu the next time a reply is slow?
qa.a: Lavanya could ask gently what else might explain the silence, like tuition or a flat phone, and suggest waiting a little before deciding anything. Sitting with Charu while she waits also helps.

qa.q: Why is Lavanya unsure what was in Charu's head, and what does she go by?
qa.a: Lavanya can only see the outside: the checking under the table, the tight knees and the lack of tears. Lavanya reads these as signs of fear because she knows Charu well, but can't be certain.

grounding: An older sister watches a fourteen-year-old decide from one slow reply that her friend is bored of her and she will be left alone.

passage:
The group discussion round at the Lucknow campus had lasted twelve minutes, and Reena had spoken for maybe forty seconds. When the list went up, her roll number wasn't on it.

On the walk to the metro, her mind moved fast. If I can't pass a group discussion, I can't pass anything. Every company has one. So no job this year. Then everyone gets placed but me. Papa will stop mentioning me to his friends. Chachi will ask at every wedding. I'll be twenty-five and still at home, filling forms.

It felt like a perfectly logical chain.

Yusuf caught up with her at the ticket gate. "You okay? That was just the first company."

"It's not about one company," Reena said. "It's about what it shows."

"What does it show?"

She opened her mouth and realised she couldn't answer without jumping straight to the wedding.

qa.a: Reena had spoken for maybe forty seconds.

qa.q: Why does Reena's chain of thoughts feel logical to her?

qa.q: What was the turning point at the ticket gate, and what could Reena do next?
qa.a: Yusuf's simple question, "What does it show?", made her notice she had skipped straight to the wedding. Next she could write down the actual steps between one lost round and never being employed.

qa.q: How might Yusuf see Reena's reaction to one list?
qa.a: Yusuf sees one company and one round, so Reena's sadness may seem bigger than the event. Yusuf seems to care enough to ask rather than argue.

"How was the interview?" Disha asked. She had come home early from her office to hear.

"Gone. I blanked on the coding question."

"Okay. So that company's gone."

"Not just that company, Didi. If I blank there, I'll blank everywhere. Then no job. Then Baba takes that loan for nothing. Then I'm the son who sits at home while Rinku's son is in Bengaluru."

passage:
I'm Seema. Last winter at the logistics firm in Kochi, I watched my colleague Jomon take one small mistake and build a disaster out of it.

He'd sent the monthly delivery report to the regional head with one wrong date: the 31st of November. He saw it an hour later and went grey. "That's it. She'll think I'm careless. My probation review is next month. They won't confirm me. And then who hires someone who didn't pass probation?"

I didn't tell him to relax. People said that to me once and it made me want to throw a stapler. I asked, "What's the worst realistic thing that happens today?"

He thought. "She replies and points it out."

"And how likely is it that one date decides your probation?"

A long breath. "Not very. My numbers are fine."

We wrote a one-line correction together. He sent it, then went to get tea for both of us.

qa.q: What wrong date did Jomon put in the report?
qa.a: The 31st of November.

qa.q: Why did the mistake feel career-ending to Jomon when he saw it?
qa.a: His probation review was coming up, so any slip seemed like proof he would fail it. Fear pulled one wrong date forward into not being confirmed and not being hired.

qa.q: Why did Seema's questions work better than telling Jomon to relax?
qa.a: Asking about the worst realistic outcome and how likely it was made Jomon reason it out himself. He reached "not very" on his own, which shrank the disaster more than reassurance would.

qa.q: How might Jomon have felt if Seema had simply said "relax"?
qa.a: He might have felt brushed off and more alone with the fear, the way Seema once did. The steady questions showed that Seema took him seriously.

grounding: A colleague sees a peer treat a wrong date in a report as the end of his job and asks about the worst realistic outcome and its likelihood.

Peer-buddy note, research lab, Thursday

Akash has been in the lab six weeks. Today he found that a table in his weekly summary to Prof. Menon listed a reading in millilitres instead of microlitres. The calculations below were correct; only the unit label was wrong.

He came to my bench, very pale. "She'll think I can't be trusted with data. She'll take me off the project. I'll have to leave the PhD." He was talking faster and faster.

I asked him to sit. Then two questions: "What is the worst thing that could realistically happen this week?" and "How likely is it?"

He said, slowly, that she might ask him to fix the table. And that she had corrected her own units in last month's meeting.

We sent a two-line correction together. He was quiet for a while afterwards, still embarrassed, but he went back to his pipettes.

Next step: I'll check in on Monday and share my own checklist for units.

— Aparna

qa.q: What unit was wrongly written in Akash's table?
qa.a: It listed millilitres instead of microlitres.

qa.q: What does Akash talking faster and faster suggest about his state of mind?
qa.a: It suggests fear was running ahead of him, turning one wrong label into leaving the PhD. He seemed caught in the spiral rather than thinking through the facts.

qa.q: What small step did Aparna take that helped, and why?
qa.a: Aparna had Akash sit and answer two questions about the worst realistic outcome and its likelihood. Slowing down let him notice that Prof. Menon had fixed her own units recently.

qa.q: How might Prof. Menon see the two-line correction?
qa.a: Prof. Menon would most likely see it as a careful student catching a small error, not as untrustworthiness. Having fixed her own units last month, she probably understands.

grounding: A lab peer sees a new student treat a unit mistake as the end of his PhD and uses calm questions about realistic outcomes to shrink the fear.

passage:
Indu, you asked how I survived opening night. I'll tell you exactly. I'm Vaibhav, and three nights before it, I couldn't eat.

I'm the new sound person at the theatre, and all I could see was the mic dying in the middle of the big speech, four hundred people staring at the sound booth. Me.

So on Wednesday I did something my old teacher taught me. I wrote the fear at the top of a page: "The lead's mic fails." Under it, "What would I do?" Spare mic in my pocket, already tested. Fade up the stage mics. Signal the stage manager. Then, "How likely?" We'd had one glitch in twelve rehearsals, and that was a loose cable I've since taped down.

I did the same for the laptop crashing. Backup track on my phone.

The fear didn't vanish. But it went from a cloud to a list. And on the night, nothing failed.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav keep as a backup in case the lead's mic failed?
qa.a: A spare mic, already tested.

qa.q: Why could Vaibhav not eat three nights before the show?
qa.a: Vaibhav was picturing the worst moment, the mic dying with four hundred people staring at the sound booth, and it felt as if nothing could be done. The dread was vague and huge.

qa.q: What was the turning point in how Vaibhav handled the fear?
qa.a: Writing the fear down and answering "What would I do?" and "How likely?" under it. Having a plan and a real number turned the cloud into a list Vaibhav could act on.

qa.q: How might Indu react to hearing that nothing failed on the night?
qa.a: Indu might be relieved and a bit amused that all that worry ended in a smooth show. Indu may also want to borrow the method for another fear.

grounding: A young adult writes down a feared failure, what could be done about it and how likely it is, and the dread becomes a manageable plan.

I share a flat with Sarika in Mysuru. She runs a small Bharatanatyam class for children in a rented hall, and last month the owner hinted the rent might go up.

For a week she was different. She'd sit with her tea going cold. Once I heard her say, to nobody, "That's it, the class is finished."

Then one night I found her at the dining table with a sheet of paper in three columns. I read the headings upside down: "If the rent goes up", "What I could do", "How likely". Under the middle one she'd written: ask the owner directly, look at the temple hall, raise fees slightly with notice, share the hall with Revathi's music class.

I didn't ask much. She said, "It's still scary. But now it's a to-do list, not a cliff." The next morning she called the owner.

I can't say how she really felt. But she sang while cooking that evening.

— Irawati

qa.q: Where did Irawati find Sarika one night?
qa.a: At the dining table with a sheet of paper in three columns.

qa.q: What did Sarika mean by "now it's a to-do list, not a cliff"?
qa.a: She meant the fear still existed, but writing down options made it feel like something she could act on rather than a sudden fall. Having choices eased the helplessness.

qa.q: What would you advise Sarika if the owner does raise the rent?
qa.a: Go back to the middle column and try the options one by one, starting with the temple hall or sharing with Revathi's class. The list she already made is her plan.

qa.q: Why can Irawati only guess how Sarika really felt?
qa.a: Irawati sees behaviour, like cold tea, the columns and singing while cooking, but not Sarika's inner thoughts. Irawati reads the singing as a good sign without being sure.

grounding: A flatmate watches a young woman write down a feared rent rise, what she could do and how likely it is, and move from dread to action.

The cast list for the spring play was taped to the classroom door in Nairobi. Gabriel, nine, read it three times. Twenty-two names. Not his.

At home, he dropped his bag by the sofa. His sister Amara looked up from her maths.

"Ms Wanjiru thinks I'm useless," Gabriel said. "That's why."

"Did she say that?"

"She doesn't need to. When she read the list out she didn't even look at me. She looked at the window. And last week she made me redo my handwriting."

"She makes everyone redo handwriting."

"Not like me. She hates me. It's a fact."

Gabriel went to his room and lay facing the wall, sure of what Ms Wanjiru was thinking. It didn't occur to him that there were only twenty-two parts and twenty-eight children in the class.

qa.a: Twenty-two names.

You want to know why I stopped wearing that dupatta, Apa? Fine. I'm Zainab, and it's stupid, but here.

It was Ammi's old one, the orange one with a small burn mark near the edge. I liked it. I wore it to the school exhibition on Saturday.

I walked in, and Aditi leaned over to Gunjan and whispered something. Gunjan covered her mouth. That was all I needed. I knew what Aditi said. "Look, she's wearing a curtain." I could hear it in her exact voice, the one she uses for mocking.

I folded the dupatta into my bag in the washroom and spent the whole exhibition feeling cold and plain. I didn't look at them once.

I'm Nandini, in Class 10 at the girls' school in Hubballi. On Monday, Farida came in wearing a hand-knitted school sweater, a slightly brighter blue than everyone else's. Right then, Deepali leaned over and whispered to me, "Did you finish question six? I got minus forty." I laughed, because minus forty on a speed question is ridiculous.

I saw Farida freeze. She sat down, pulled the sweater off and stuffed it into her bag, even though the fan was on and the room was cold. For the whole maths period she sat with her arms crossed. At lunch she sat with her back to us.

I think she was sure we were laughing at her sweater. I can't know for certain. But her face went red at the exact second I laughed, and she never looked our way.

On Tuesday she came without it, shivering. I finally went over. "Farida, we were laughing at Deepali's maths, not you. The sweater's nice." She stared at me for a long time. "Really?"

qa.q: What was Deepali whispering about?
qa.a: Deepali asked, "Did you finish question six? I got minus forty."

qa.q: Why did Farida pull the sweater off even though the room was cold?
qa.a: She seemed sure the laughter was about her sweater and felt embarrassed. Hiding it felt safer than being mocked, even if she was cold.

qa.q: What choice did Nandini make that could change things, and why does it help?
qa.a: Nandini went over and told Farida what the whisper was really about. That gave Farida real information to replace the story she had imagined.

qa.q: What was it like for Nandini to watch Farida sit with her arms crossed all period?
qa.a: Nandini seems to have felt uneasy and a bit guilty, guessing her laugh had been misread. It took until Tuesday for her to decide to go over and clear it up.

grounding: A classmate watches a teenage girl become certain that a whisper and a laugh were mocking her sweater, without ever checking.

passage:
I'm Kavitha. It was the evening after our college hackathon; I'd been awake for almost thirty hours. I got back to our girls' PG and lay on the bed in my jeans.

Ayesha came in bouncing. "Okay, Holi plan! Terrace at ten, natural colours only, I'll make thandai, and then we all go to Meenu's for lunch."

"Mm," I said, with my eyes closed.

She stopped. "Wow. You clearly hate it. You could just say you don't want to come."

It stung, because I hadn't said anything like that. For a second I wanted to snap back, "Stop putting words in my mouth." But I was too tired to fight, which actually helped.

I opened one eye. "Ayesha, I love the plan. I'm just so tired I can't feel my feet. Can you tell me again tomorrow?"

She looked at me, at the jeans, at the hackathon badge still round my neck. "Oh. Sleep, idiot."

I was asleep before she switched off the light.

qa.q: How long had Kavitha been awake?
qa.a: Almost thirty hours.

qa.q: Why did Ayesha's words sting Kavitha?
qa.a: Kavitha felt misread: she hadn't said anything against the plan, and being told she hated it put words in her mouth. Being tired made the unfairness sharper.

qa.q: What worked about how Kavitha answered instead of snapping back?

Volunteer coordinator's note, college NSS unit, Friday

Planning meeting for next month's village camp. Santosh presented the route and the tree-planting schedule with a lot of energy. Hansa sat at the end of the table, very quiet, and didn't take notes.

Halfway through, Santosh stopped and said, "Hansa, you obviously think this plan is useless. Just say it." The room went silent.

Hansa looked startled and then hurt. I could see her deciding whether to argue. Instead she said, quite gently, "I don't think it's useless. I came straight off the overnight bus from my grandmother's and I'm running on nothing. I actually like the tree part."

Santosh went red and said sorry. Hansa smiled a little, but stayed quiet for the rest of the meeting, and I noticed she rubbed her eyes several times.

Next step: I'll suggest to both of them that we check in with people before reading faces in meetings, and ask Hansa to lead the tree-planting group.

— Coordinator

qa.q: What schedule did Santosh present at the meeting?
qa.a: The route and the tree-planting schedule.

qa.q: What did Hansa seem to feel when Santosh said she thought the plan was useless?
qa.a: She seemed startled and hurt at being misread, and maybe tempted to argue back. Her tiredness from the overnight bus was being taken as dislike.

qa.q: What would you advise Santosh the next time someone is quiet in a meeting?
qa.a: Ask a simple question, like "How are you finding it?", instead of announcing what the person thinks. It gives them space to say what's really going on.

qa.q: If you were Hansa, what would you want from the group after this?
qa.a: Probably for people to take her word that she was tired, not critical, and to be given a real part, like leading the tree group. Being trusted would ease the sting.

grounding: A coordinator records a young woman who was tired and quiet being told she thinks the plan is useless, and how she gently says what she actually feels.

By Thursday afternoon at the ad agency in Andheri, Kashish had built a whole story. Sachin hadn't laughed at her joke in the stand-up. He'd answered her draft with "noted." He'd eaten lunch at his desk instead of joining them.

He thinks I stole the tea-brand pitch idea, she thought. He's going to say it in Monday's review. She'd already rehearsed three replies in the washroom mirror.

At four she caught herself drafting a fourth. Enough. She walked over to his desk.

"Sachin, can I ask something? Are you annoyed with me about the pitch? I'd rather ask than keep guessing."

He looked up, surprised. "What? No! My landlord's selling the flat and I have to move by the fifteenth. I've been apartment-hunting on my phone all day. Sorry, I've been a zombie."

The whole thing took two minutes. Kashish went back to her desk and deleted the fourth reply.

qa.q: What did Sachin answer Kashish's draft with?
qa.a: He'd answered her draft with "noted."

qa.q: Why did Kashish's story about Sachin feel so convincing to her?
qa.a: Each small sign, the missed laugh, the short reply and the lunch at his desk, seemed to fit one explanation. Rehearsing replies in the mirror made the imagined conflict feel even more real.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and why did it work so quickly?
qa.a: Kashish caught herself drafting a fourth reply and decided to ask Sachin directly. One two-minute question replaced days of guessing with his actual reason.

qa.q: How might Sachin have felt when Kashish asked if he was annoyed?
qa.a: Sachin was surprised, and maybe a little relieved to explain why he'd been so distracted. He might also have felt bad that his stress had come across as coldness.

grounding: A young woman who is sure a colleague is annoyed with her asks him directly, and a two-minute question replaces hours of imagined conversation.

Tea break at the tea estate office, Darjeeling. Dolma waited until the others had gone out to the verandah.

"Anirban-da, do you have a minute?"

"Hmm?" He didn't look up from the ledger.

"You've been very quiet with me since Tuesday. You didn't come to see the new drying racks with me. I've been wondering if I did something."

He looked up. "You? No."

"I thought maybe the racks report. I changed your figures."

"You fixed them. I was glad." He rubbed his eyes. "My mother's been unwell. I've been at the hospital at night. I'm not with anyone, Dolma. I'm barely here."

"Oh." Dolma sat down. "I've spent three days writing arguments with you in my head."

He almost smiled. "Did I win?"

"Every time." She pushed her cup towards him. "Drink this. I'll show you the racks tomorrow."

qa.q: What did Dolma think Anirban might be upset about?
qa.a: The racks report, where she changed his figures.

qa.q: What does "I've spent three days writing arguments with you in my head" show about Dolma's state before she asked?
qa.a: It shows she was anxious and sure she had upset him, building imagined conflicts for days. Her guess felt real enough to argue with.

qa.q: Which choice of Dolma's made the difference, and why?
qa.a: Waiting until they were alone and asking plainly whether she had done something. It gave Anirban the chance to tell her the real reason in a minute.

qa.q: How might Anirban feel after Dolma asks him directly?
qa.a: Anirban may feel relieved to share what's going on with his mother, and touched that Dolma cared enough to ask. His small joke suggests some of the weight lifted.

grounding: A young woman sure her colleague is annoyed asks him directly at the tea break and learns his quietness has nothing to do with her.
